L41: Species: Dog

L43: Area of Study: Medical Oncology
L44: Purpose of Study: The purpose of this study is to provide a direct comparison between the outcomes for dogs with peripheral T cell lymphoma (PTCL) treated with CHOP or LOPP chemotherapy. The findings of this study could help veterinarians understand if one protocol is truly superior to the other for dogs with PTCL.
L45: 
L46: In this study, your dog will be randomly selected to receive either CHOP or LOPP chemotherapy. At each visit, their lymph node size, blood work, and overall wellbeing will be assessed.
L47: Timeline: Both protocols involve treatments every 7–14 days and take 4-6 months to complete. Following protocol completion, your pet will return once monthly to assess remission status.
L48: 
L49: Eligibility: Your dog may qualify if:
L50:   * Confirmed peripheral T cell lymphoma diagnosis via cytology or histopathology
L51:     * No indolent forms of lymphoma, such as T zone lymphoma
L52:     * Cutaneous lymphoma will not be included
L53:   * No prior chemotherapy or radiation therapy for lymphoma. It is preferred that patients are not started on steroids in advance of enrollment. However, if deemed by the overseeing clinician, patients can still be enrolled on steroids for up to 10 days.
L54:   * No major lab work abnormalities that prevent chemotherapy administration
L55:   * No evidence of dilated cardiomyopathy, ventricular arrhythmia, or liver failure
L56: ## T Cell Diagnostic Testing
L57: 
L58: A diagnosis of T cell lymphoma can be made using one or more of the following tests:
L59: 
L60:   * Immunocytochemistry (ICC)*
L61:   * Immunohistochemistry (IHC)*
L62:   * PCR for antigen receptor rearrangements (PARR)*
L63:   * Flow cytometry
L64: 
L65: *Available through the 【12†MSU Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory†vdl.msu.edu】
L66: 
L67: Client Benefits: This is a partially funded trial.
L68:   * A test must be conducted to confirm the T cell lymphoma diagnosis in study participants. T cell diagnostic testing can be conducted at MSU or through clients’ primary care veterinarians. Diagnostic testing at MSU costs approximately $250. For dogs accepted to the study, the cost will be reimbursed by an account credit at the MSU Veterinary Medical Center at trial completion (either when the protocol is completed or the patient develops progressive disease).
L69:   * Initial evaluation appointments will be charged. For dogs accepted to the study, recheck exams during clinical trial appointments will be free of cost ($60 value per visit). Costs associated with blood work and treatment will remain the responsibility of the client (with the exception described below).
L70:   * Dogs will receive the first dose of doxorubicin (for those assigned to the CHOP protocol) or lomustine (for those assigned to the LOPP protocol) free of cost. First-dose administrative and blood work fees also will be free of cost.
L71:   * Clients are financially responsible for all treatments and diagnostics that are unrelated to the study.
L72: Client Responsibilities:
L73:   * To administer prednisone, chemotherapy, or supplemental medications as prescribed by the attending veterinarian.
L74:   * To comply with the visit schedule outlined by study investigators
L75:   * To report any abnormal behavior or signs of illness to study investigators.
L76:   * To contact study investigators if your dog is evaluated by any other veterinarians during the course of the study.
L77:   * To inform study investigators of any non-study-related veterinary treatments recommended for your dog during the course of the study.

L55: Purpose of the study:
L56: Histiocytic sarcoma is an aggressive cancer in dogs that often does not respond well to standard treatments like chemotherapy or radiation. While some dogs experience benefits, these treatments affect many cells at once and cannot adapt as a tumor changes. New research shows that cancer closely interacts with the immune system and surrounding tissues, suggesting that better treatments may need to work inside cells, not just target them from the outside.
L57: Quasiorganelle therapy is an experimental approach that aims to do this by using weakened, non-disease-causing bacteria derived from Listeria monocytogenes to deliver helpful genetic instructions directly into immune and tumor cells, with the goal of improving how the body recognizes and responds to cancer.
L58: The aim of this study is to determine whether quasiorganelle therapy can be given safely to dogs with histiocytic sarcoma and to determine an appropriate dosing schedule. The treatment has been tested in laboratory and preclinical studies but not yet in dogs with naturally-occurring cancer. Because animals with cancer may respond differently than healthy animals, this study also looks for early biological or clinical signs that the therapy may be beneficial.
L59: 
L60: Inclusion criteria:
L61:   * Confirmed diagnosis of histiocytic sarcoma, including hemophagocytic histiocytic sarcoma, as determined by immune marker expression.
L62:   * Visible tumor at the time of enrollment.
L63:     * Up to 5 lesions
L64:     * Sum of the longest lesion dimensions <15cm
L65:   * Adequate organ function indicated by standard laboratory tests.
L66:   * Minimum weight requirement of 20 kg (44 lbs).
L67:   * VCOG performance status up to 2.
L68: 
L69: Exclusion criteria:
L70:   * Concurrent diseases such as: diabetes mellitus, Addison’s disease (hypoadrenocorticism), Cushing’s disease (hyperadrenocorticism), kidney disease
L71:   * Active wounds.
L72:   * Concurrent medications such as: immunosuppressants (including corticosteroids, cyclosporine, azathioprine, mycophenolate) or systemic antibiotics within 14 days.
L73:   * Neutropenia, immunodeficiency, or immune-mediated disease
L74:   * Prior anti-cancer treatment
L75:     * Corticosteroid (prednisone) within 7 days.
L76:     * Chemotherapy within 14 days.
L77:     * Radiation therapy within 30 days.
L78: Treatment:
L79: The first group (8 dogs) will receive quasiorganelle therapy alone. Their tumor will be measured and they will receive the quasiorganelle infusion. They will then be observed for up 4 days at the MSU Veterinary Medical Center and blood and fecal samples will be taken at set timepoints. The dogs will return for treatment once weekly for 4 doses followed by 2 weeks off. This schedule will then be repeated two more times for a total of 16 weeks of treatment.
L80: Imaging to determine alterations in tumor size will be repeated at the end of each 4 week treatment period.
L81: The second group (8 dogs) will receive quaisorganelle therapy that includes gene therapy. Their treatment and monitoring schedule will be identical to that of the first group.
L82: 
L83: Following the 16 week treatment period, dogs will return for evaluation every 4 weeks or until progressive disease is documented.
L84: 
L85: Please note: While enrolled, dogs should not live with anyone who is pregnant or planning to become pregnant.
L86: 
L87: Compensation:
L88:   * This is a funded trial. All tests and treatments associated with the trial will be covered once a dog is enrolled.
L89:   * Complications associated with the trial will be covered. Clients are financially responsible for all treatments and diagnostics that are unrelated to the trial. Association between complications and trial treatment will be determined by the overseeing clinician and investigators.
L90:   * Initial evaluation appointments will be charged.
L91:   * Quasiorganelle therapy (with or without gene therapy) will be administered free of cost. Hospitalization immediately following administration and associated treatments will be free of cost. Blood and fecal sampling and imaging studies associated with the trial will be free of cost.
L92: Contact information: Please feel free to contact our Medical Oncology Team at (517) 353-5420 or cvm.oncoinfo@msu.edu to refer a patient or for any additional information. Referring veterinarian and client calls are welcome.

L53: Clinical Study: Time to Maximal Response to Neoadjuvant Corticosteroids in Dogs with Mast Cell Tumors
L54: 
L55: Purpose of Study:
L56: Mast cell tumors (MCT) are the most common skin tumor in dogs. MCTs can be treated in a variety of ways, with surgery being a common component of care. When MCTs are located in a challenging surgical location, we will try pre-treating with drugs to shrink the tumor and give the surgeon more flexibility. Historically, these pre-surgical treatments include chemotherapy and/or corticosteroids. Anecdotally, if the MCT shrinks, the effect only lasts for a limited period.
L57: To date, there are no studies identifying the ideal time between starting steroids and performing surgery. In this study, we plan to identify canine patients with cutaneous MCTs, administer corticosteroids, and before proceeding to surgery, clients (pet owners) will obtain daily measurements.
L58: The aim of this study is to identify guidelines for pre-operative steroid treatment with secondary goals of decreasing surgical risks and improving post-operative outcomes in dogs affected by this disease. Identifying an ideal pre-surgical treatment window can improve veterinarian confidence in surgical scheduling, help facilitate successful surgery, and limit the influence of steroids on wound healing.
L59: 
L60: Eligibility Criteria:
L61:   * Inclusion criteria:
L62:     * Confirmed mast cell tumor diagnosis via cytology or histopathology (may be completed through primary veterinarian or at MSU)
L63:     * Cutaneous mast cell tumor located on the trunk (above the elbow or knee)
L64:     * Mast cell tumor measures between 2-6cm in one dimension
L65:     * Bloodwork confirming adequate organ function and ability to undergo general anesthesia (may be completed through primary veterinarian or at MSU)
L66:   * Exclusion criteria:
L67:     * Prior anti-cancer treatment, including steroids, within 7 days
L68:     * Patients on NSAIDs need 5 or more days of washout before enrolling
L69:     * Evidence of MCT metastasis
L70:     * Expected survival < 4 weeks with treatment
L71:     * Diabetes mellitus or other systemic condition that interferes with safe steroid administration
L72: Eligibility Diagnostics:
L73: 
L74: Prior to study entry, pet owners will be responsible for an initial consultation at MSU and to complete the following diagnostics for their dog:
L75: 
L76:   * Cytology or histopathology of tumor in question to confirm diagnosis of MCT (if not already completed)
L77:   * Bloodwork ensuring adequate organ function to undergo general anesthesia (if not already completed)
L78: Staging diagnostics including abdominal ultrasound with cytologic evaluation of regional lymph nodes, spleen, and/or liver will be contingent on a overseeing clinician’s recommendation as well as client election. This is not a requirement for inclusion.
L79: 
L80: Treatment:
L81: Initial caliper measurements of the tumor will be obtained by 2 trained staff members on the day of enrollment. Clients will be trained by MSU staff in caliper usage and each dog will be prescribed prednisone, diphenhydramine, and either famotidine or omeprazole for 14 days.
L82: Each morning, the clients will obtain caliper measurements of the MCT in the 3 planes as instructed per specific training images. Photographs that include the caliper will be emailed to the primary investigators daily. In-person evaluations will be completed at MSU on days 7 and 14 to confirm measurement accuracy and allow for surgical planning.
L83: Surgical resection will be planned for Day 14 (+/- 1 day) with the MSU Soft Tissue Surgery service, and tissue will be submitted for biopsy analysis. Patients who experience significant or rapid tumor shrinkage may undergo surgery sooner.
L84: 
L85: If at any time throughout treatment, the tumor grows by >20%, the patient will be removed from the trial and given appropriate care based on clinician discretion.
L86: 
L87: Compensation:
L88:   * This is a partially funded trial
L89:     * Up to 50% of the surgical fees and the histopathology fees will be covered
L90:     * All trial-specific medications (prednisone, diphenhydramine, famotidine/omeprazole) will be covered once enrolled
L91:     * Calipers will be provided
L92:   * If additional surgery is completed under the same anesthetic event, the client will be financially responsible

L57: Study Title: Efficacy and safety of a novel anti-cancer therapeutic for the treatment of metastatic mammary carcinoma in cats
L58: Purpose of Study: Mammary tumors are a commonly encountered cancer in cats, particularly in females, with 80-90% of masses diagnosed as malignant (carcinoma). Mammary carcinoma in cats parallels breast cancer in humans with regards to receptor expression profile and propensity of metastasis. The median survival time in cats ranges from 6 months to several years, depending on tumor size and grade. Greater than 60% of cats have more than one tumor at diagnosis, with the majority being high grade.
L59: The objective of this study is to evaluate the safety and efficacy of a novel therapeutic targeting miR-10b, a molecule responsible for viability of metastatic cells in cats with mammary carcinoma. This multipurpose therapy has a previously demonstrated efficacy in halting breast cancer invasion and metastasis in mice. The advantage of our novel therapeutic over existing drugs is that it can also be used to visualize primary and metastatic lesions in vivo by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
L60: Studies in cats with mammary carcinoma will help bring this therapeutic into clinic to treat human breast cancer.
L61: Inclusion Criteria (may be evaluated at MSU or at primary care):
L62:   * Histologic or cytologic diagnosis confirmatory of mammary carcinoma with metastasis
L63:   * Diagnosis of metastatic lesions confirmed via cytology/histopathology if accessible, or based on clinical suspicion
L64:   * Non-ulcerated primary/external mammary carcinoma lesions, total volume up to 8 cm^{3}, subject to the overall health evaluation
L65:   * Overall health criteria, adequate liver function, adequate renal function, expected survival >4 weeks
L66:   * Lymph node metastasis, or any other metastatic invasion to be confirmed by cytology and/or CT scan
L67:   * Cases that have not undergone surgery or have undergone unilateral or bilateral mastectomy with metastatic involvement will be included
L68:   * Tumors with or without prior chemotherapy, concurrent NSAIDs are allowed
L69:   * Confirmed microRNA-10b overexpression > log 2 in lesion vs non-tumor parenchyma
L70:   * Informed client consent signed and willingness to consent to drug administration at multiple intervals, blood draws, return visits, monthly CT scans, post-mortem examination
L71: Study Treatment: Cats with metastatic mammary carcinoma will first undergo a baseline CT scan. Cats will also undergo diagnostic imaging (MRI) before and 24 hours after the injection of the therapeutic to ensure its accumulation in the tumor lesion(s). For all imaging (MRI or CT scan) cats will be maintained under anesthesia using routine anesthesia methods and will be monitored closely by veterinary specialists.
L72: After the first injection, treatment will be repeated in two weeks followed by monthly CT scans and treatments. The follow up period may be extended for up to 12 months after initial treatments based on response.
L73: Compensation: This is a funded study: cats will receive the investigational therapeutic and associated imaging free of cost. Pet owners are financially responsible for all treatments and diagnostics that are unrelated to the study.

-A New Drug for Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma in Dogs
-Canine
-Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) is the second most common oral malignant tumor in dogs. They are locally invasive and often recurrent. They invade the bone rapidly and sometimes cannot be removed by surgery.
-Trametinib is an oral medication approved by the FDA for use in certain types of cancer in humans and has been previously found to be safe in dogs under experimental conditions. We have found that some dogs with oral squamous cell carcinomas respond very favorably to the drug, while others do not. This is an expanded study to learn more about why some of these cancers respond well so we can target therapy most effectively.
-Eligibility:
-Dogs seen by the Cornell University Hospital for Animals (CUHA) who have been diagnosed with an oral squamous cell carcinoma are eligible.
-Compensation:
-All visits and procedures directly related to and during the study will be performed entirely free of charge to you. The drug will also be provided to you free of charge. Additionally, if your dog completes the study, the study will cover an additional $1000 worth of medical expenses related to standard of care therapy for your dog's SCC.
-Owner Responsibilities:
-We will ask you to bring your dog to the CUHA for follow up appointments on or around days 14, 42, 70, 108, and 126 after enrollment. On days 14, 42, 70 and 108 we will conduct a physical and oral examination under light sedation. On day 126, we will do a physical exam and perform a full-body CT scan under general anesthesia to document response to treatment, obtain a tumor tissue sample and perform a fine-needle aspirate of the mandibular (under the jaw) lymph nodes for microscopic and genetic analyses.
-You are also committing to sharing clinical information by means of a short questionnaire to be completed at each visit, or by attending a short weekly phone call to allow us to closely monitor and document any side effects.
-Finally, you are committing to give the medicine by mouth once daily. This medication is considered chemotherapy and safety instructions will be relayed to you. We will also ask you to complete a brief questionnaire about your dog's health once a week (either over the phone or in person at the visits).

protocol.tagline: Help us test a new treatment for advanced bone cancer in dogs.
protocol.description:
This study is evaluating a new type of cancer treatment called CAR T cell therapy for dogs with osteosarcoma that has spread to the lungs.

CAR T cell therapy uses your dog’s own immune cells to help fight cancer. A blood sample is collected (about 3-4 tablespoons), and special immune cells (called T cells) are modified in a lab to better recognize and attack cancer cells. These upgraded cells are then given back to your dog through an IV infusion.

Dogs in this study will also receive medications to prepare the body for treatment and to support the immune system during the study. The goal is to determine if this treatment is safe and effective for dogs with metastatic bone cancer.

protocol.name: Fluorescence Imaging with PDL1-IRDye800 to Guide Surgical Treatment of Oral Cancer in Dogs
protocol.tagline: New theragnostic agent (diagnostic and therapeutic) to improve our ability to effectively treat oral cancer!
protocol.description:
For dogs diagnosed with oral cancer (Squamous Cell Carcinoma, Oral Malignant Melanoma), curative intent surgical removal has been consistently found to have the longest remission rate. However, conventional diagnostic imaging, which we use to plan our surgery, is imperfect and can underestimate the extent of the tumor which results in the potential that not all cancer cells are removed during surgery. This directly impacts patient outcomes (disease free interval and overall survival). There is a critical need to improve our ability to detect cancer intraoperatively (i.e. during the surgery) to improve patient outcomes.


Further, for human head and neck cancer the standard of care is to give immunotherapy (drugs that improve the immune system's ability to fight off cancer) prior to surgery, which has resulted in increased survival in a subset of patients. We have no data on this type of pre-surgical treatment in dogs, and if it would also improve patient survival times.


The purpose of this study is to evaluate the use of a theranostic agent (diagnostic and therapeutic) before surgery to improve our ability to effectively treat oral cancer. protocol.description:
About 3 in 100 dogs are diagnosed with brain tumors each year, and gliomas are among the hardest to treat because they can escape traditional treatments. This study is focused on finding new treatment options for dogs with brain tumors, specifically gliomas, which are one of the most difficult types to treat. Researchers are exploring a new approach called immunotherapy, which helps the body’s own immune system fight cancer.


In this study, a small blood sample is taken from your dog to collect immune cells (called T cells). These cells are then modified in the lab to better recognize and attack cancer cells. The upgraded cells (called CAR T cells) are given back to your dog to target the tumor.


Dogs in this study will also receive a chemotherapy drug called verdinexor, which may help improve the effectiveness of the treatment.


Additionally, dogs can receive radiation therapy, which is currently the gold-standard for treating gliomas in dogs. We hope that by attacking the tumor through immunotherapy, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy, we will give dogs the best chance at success.


This is the first study to test this type of therapy in dogs, building on promising results seen in children with brain tumors.

protocol.description:
This study is evaluating a new limb-sparing surgery for dogs with bone cancer (osteosarcoma). Instead of removing the limb, this approach uses a custom 3D-printed implant to replace the diseased bone.

-Up to 90% of thyroid tumors in dogs are cancerous, and the main treatment right now is  surgery.  The thyroid sits next to critical blood vessels and breathing tubes, creating potential complications for surgery. Furthermore, many tumors cannot be operated on at all because they are stuck to these vital structures.  Histotripsy is an innovative method using focused sound waves—not heat, surgery, or radiation—to safely destroy tumor cells with millimeter accuracy. Prior studies using this technology for canine bone cancer were safe and successful.  Histotripsy has the potential to be the first truly tissue-selective ablation method capable of sparing nerves, vessels, and other critical structures for thyroid tumor ablation

-Purpose
-This study aims to determine if it is safe and feasible to use a light-sensitive drug called verteporfin, in combination with photodynamic therapy (PDT), in dogs with newly diagnosed brain tumors.
-Background
-Canine brain tumors generally respond poorly to standard treatments, including surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy.  Researchers are now testing a new treatment called photodynamic therapy (PDT) for human brain tumors in Germany and France.  This therapy uses a special drug, verteporfin, that is activated by laser light to specifically kill cancer cells, leaving healthy tissue untouched.
-In this study, we’re testing PDT in dogs who’ve been diagnosed with brain tumors. Our goal is to find out if PDT can be done safely, and see if it helps destroy the tumor cells that can often remain following tumor removal surgery.
-Eligibility
-Dogs newly diagnosed with a brain tumor confirmed with MRI scan or tumor biopsy that can be surgically removed
-Dogs stable enough for surgery and general anesthesia
-Exclusion Criteria
-Dogs that have received chemotherapy, radiation, or other therapies for brain tumors
-Dogs with severe systemic disease or not stable to undergo surgery and anesthesia
-Study Design
-To take part in this study, dogs must be newly diagnosed with a brain tumor, confirmed based on an MRI scan or tumor biopsy.
-If your dog qualifies:
-While your dog is under general anesthesia for brain surgery, the surgeon will remove as much of the tumor as possible.
-Your dog will receive a drug called verteporfin, which makes tumor cells sensitive to light. The drug is given by injection into a vein during surgery.
-After the tumor is removed, a laser light will be shined on the surgical area. This light activates the verteporfin, which helps kill any tumor cells that might remain.
-To better understand how this drug works in dogs, we will collect five small blood samples within two hours of giving the injection.
-After surgery and PDT treatment, your dog will stay in the hospital for approximately 2–3 days to recover before going home.
-As part of the study, your dog will have follow-up visits for about 6 months, unless you choose to withdraw your dog, or your dog’s condition changes and he or she is no longer able to safely undergo anesthesia or follow-up procedures.
-If you decide to pursue other treatment options, you can withdraw your dog from the study at any time.
-Study Visits
-Your dog will need to come to the Virginia-Maryland College of Veterinary Medicine in Blacksburg, VA for the following visits:
-Day 1: Enrollment, physical exam, and lab work.
-Day 2: Brain surgery, PDT treatment with verteporfin, blood sampling, and post-treatment MRI.
-Day 14: Recheck visit — physical exam and lab work.
-Days 42, 84, and 180: Recheck visits — physical exam, lab work, and brain MRI under anesthesia.
-You will be responsible for bringing your dog to all required recheck exams. The MRI scans at Days 42, 84, and 180 can typically be done as day-long, outpatient visits. However, depending on your travel distance, you and your dog may need to stay overnight.
-Compensation
-Costs associated with diagnosing your dog’s brain tumor are not covered by the study.  Once your dog is enrolled, the study covers the cost of all scheduled exams, lab tests, tumor removal surgery, anesthesia, study-related brain MRI scans, and PDT treatment. The study does not cover costs associated with treatment of brain-tumor related seizures for those dogs who have pre-existing epileptic seizures.
-Owners are responsible for travel-related expenses and medication costs associated with ongoing seizure control, if required. Some recheck appointments at your local veterinarian or neurologist may be required to monitor your dog’s health. The cost of those, along with any emergency visits that may be needed to treat seizures or other complications, are not covered by the study.

protocol.tagline: A research study evaluating a novel drug alongside radiation therapy for dogs with brain tumors.
protocol.description:
Dogs diagnosed with glioma, an aggressive brain tumor, often experience limited benefit from standard treatments such as radiation therapy alone. This clinical trial is evaluating a novel investigational drug called bisaminoquinoline-13 (BAQ-13) that may help improve how brain tumors respond to radiation therapy.


BAQ-13 works by blocking a process called autophagy, which cancer cells use to survive treatment. This study will evaluate whether BAQ-13 can safely reach brain tumors, be tolerated by dogs receiving radiation therapy, and show early signs of effectiveness.
protocol.requirements: An initial screening and eligibility workup, including physical and neurologic examination, blood work, and diagnostic imagingAdvanced brain imaging (MRI and CT scans) performed under general anesthesiaMinimally invasive brain tumor biopsies performed at enrollment and after treatmentIntravenous administration of an investigational drug (BAQ-13) twice weekly for 4 weeksConcurrent radiation therapy (standard of care)Blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample collection at specified time pointsOvernight hospitalization following biopsy proceduresFollow-up visits, including in-hospital evaluations and telemedicine check-insCompletion of owner questionnaires to monitor quality of life and treatment effectsEnd of Study: When your family is ready to elect humane euthanasia, your dog will return to UC Davis. A brief examination will be performed prior to humane euthanasia. Following your dog’s death, a brain MRI will be performed, and they will undergo a routine necropsy. We will evaluate distribution of the drug in the brain, brain tumor, and vital organs (heart, lung, kidneys, liver). If your dog passes away or is euthanized elsewhere, the study team will arrange return to UC Davis for post-mortem evaluation.
protocol.responsibilities: If you choose to enroll your dog in this study, you will be responsible for:Covering the cost of initial diagnostic tests required to determine eligibility Bringing your dog to all scheduled hospital visits, treatments, imaging appointments, and follow-up evaluationsProviding complete and accurate medical history and records as requested by the study teamCompleting quality-of-life questionnaires and participating in scheduled check-ins (including telemedicine visits)Monitoring your dog at home and promptly reporting any health changes or concerns to the study teamFollowing all study-related instructions, including medication schedules and post-procedure careCommunicating with the study team if you are unable to attend a visit or if you are considering withdrawing from the studyParticipation is voluntary, and you may withdraw your dog from the study at any time.
protocol.whoCan: Dogs may be eligible if they:Have a suspected high-grade glioma diagnosed by brain MRIAre planned to receive conventional radiation therapyAre otherwise healthy enough for anesthesia and repeated hospital visits
protocol.benefits: Potential Benefits:It is possible that this therapy may provide a benefit to your dog. Studies in mice with gliomas have demonstrated an increase in survival time after this treatment, but it is unknown whether dogs will have the same benefit. While we cannot predict if your dog will live longer with this therapy, information obtained from your dog's participation in this trial will be critical to further develop this treatment, which has the potential to lead to a breakthrough in treatment for both dogs and humans with this deadly disease.  Potential Risks:All medical procedures carry risks, and experimental treatments have the potential for increased risks because they have not been used routinely. There are two factors of this trial that carry potential risk to your dog : 1) this trial is testing a novel drug that has not been administered to pet dogs before and 2) your dog will undergo two (2) brain biopsies over the trial period. If there are complications associated with the clinical trial, the study will cover up to $3000 in medical care costs provided by the UC Davis VMTH to address complications.Novel drug therapy: Any animal or human may have an idiosyncratic (“personal”) adverse reaction to the experimental drug used in this trial. Based on the use of this treatment in healthy dogs, we believe that the risk of serious adverse effects is small. However, this study may affect your dog in ways that are unknown. These may be a minor inconvenience or may be so severe as to cause death.Brain tumor biopsy: General anesthesia is required for brain tumor biopsy, which carries inherent risk to your dog. All patients undergoing general anesthesia at the UC Davis VMC are extensively evaluated and carefully monitored during each procedure to ensure their health and safety. The biopsy procedure itself entails making a small hole in the skull and collecting 2-3 samples of tumor using a large needle. Risks associated with this procedure are low (<10% occurrence), but can include bleeding, infection, neurological decline, or even death.

protocol.description:
High-grade gliomas are aggressive brain tumors that are difficult to treat in dogs. While surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy may help some dogs, we still have much to learn about why some tumors respond better to treatment than others.


The purpose of this study is to better understand brain tumors in dogs by collecting information about each dog's health, MRI findings, tumor characteristics, and in some dogs, how they respond to radiation treatment. By studying many dogs with naturally occurring brain tumors, we hope to identify patterns that will help veterinarians diagnose these tumors more accurately, predict how they may behave, and develop more effective treatments in the future.


Although participation in this study may not directly benefit every dog, the information gained will help improve the care of dogs diagnosed with brain tumors and advance the development of new treatment options. Every dog that participates helps us learn more about brain tumors and brings us one step closer to improving treatment and quality of life for future dogs facing this disease.

protocol.name: Pilot clinical trial of anti-cancer therapy with trametinib in naturally occurring acute myeloid leukemia
protocol.tagline: Help investigate new ways to battle acute myeloid leukemia!
protocol.description:
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a fast-growing cancer of the blood and bone marrow that affects both people and dogs. Dogs diagnosed with AML usually have a poor outlook, and current treatments only extend survival for a short time, typically about 1–2 months.

Researchers are looking for better treatment options for dogs with AML. Many dogs with AML have changes (mutations) in a gene called NRAS, which can cause cancer cells to grow and survive. This study is testing a medication called trametinib, which blocks signals that cancer cells use to grow.

The purpose of this study is to find out whether trametinib is safe for dogs with AML and whether it may help slow down or reduce the cancer. Information learned from this study may also help researchers better understand leukemia in people.

This trial is being led by the Clinical Hematopathology Laboratory in partnership with the Flint Animal Cancer Center of the Colorado State University Veterinary Health System and is sponsored by the Lutsen Linder Research Fund for Extremely Gorgeous Dogs.

L54: #### ​Purpose of Study
L55: Immunotherapy, engaging the power of the immune system against cancer, has become a standard part of oncology care. One such approach utilizes the STimulator of INterferon Genes (STING) pathway. Our colleagues at University of Michigan, led by Dr. James Moon, have developed a drug that activates the STING pathway. This drug, called CMP-002, has been shown to combat cancer in a laboratory setting, with and without the use of another modulator of immune system, PD-1 blockade.
L56: This success prompted a collaboration with Michigan State University College of Veterinary Medicine as we hope to contribute to efforts that can help veterinary oncology patients and humans alike. Our initial studies, led by Dr. Vilma Yuzbasiyan-Gurkan at MSU, established the dose range tolerated in healthy dogs.
L57: The purpose of this study is to confirm the best dose of CMP-002 with or without PD-1 blockade for tumor-bearing dogs. CMP-002 has already been tested in healthy dogs. It is not uncommon for patients with cancer to process drugs differently, which is why we intend to confirm the best dose for tumor-bearing dogs. The findings of this study will then be used in future studies assessing the anti-cancer properties of CMP-002 with or without PD-1 blockade.
L58: #### Eligibility Criteria
L59:   * Inclusion criteria:
L60:     * Confirmed diagnosis of soft tissue sarcoma, lymphoma, osteosarcoma, histiocytic sarcoma, or malignant melanoma via cytology or histopathology.
L61:     * Visible tumor at the time of enrollment.
L62:     * Adequate organ function indicated by standard laboratory tests.
L63:     * Minimum weight requirement of 5 kg (11 lbs).
L64:   * Exclusion criteria:
L65:     * Prior anti-cancer treatment, including steroids, within 7 days.
L66:     * Indolent forms of lymphoma, such as T zone lymphoma.
L67:     * Expected survival < 4 weeks with treatment.
L68: #### Eligibility Diagnostics
L69: 
L70: Prior to study entry, pet owners will be charged an initial consultation fee and be financially responsible and required to have the following diagnostics performed in their dog:
L71: 
L72:   1. Diagnosis of select tumor type, if not already documented
L73:   2. Screening blood work and urinalysis, if not performed within 7 days
L74: #### Treatment
L75: The first group of patients (6–9 dogs) will receive CMP-002 alone. Their tumor will be measured and they will receive the CMP-002 infusion. They will then be observed overnight and blood samples will be taken at set timepoints. The dogs will visit their primary veterinarians one week later for blood sampling. Three weeks after the first treatment, the dogs will return to the MSU Veterinary Medical Center for a second infusion.
L76: Depending on previous response, they may be hospitalized again or sent home the same day. If tolerated, these treatments can be repeated every 3 weeks for a set number of cycles. Tumor biopsy samples may be collected at various timepoints.
L77: The second group of dogs (6–9 dogs) will receive CMP-002 with PD-1 blockade. Their tumor will measured and they will receive the CMP-002 infusion. They will then be observed overnight and blood samples will be taken at set timepoints. The dogs will return one week later for tumor measurements, blood sampling, and anti-PD-1 infusion. Three weeks after the first treatment, the dogs will return to the MSU Veterinary Medical Center for a second CMP-002 infusion.
L78: Depending on previous response, they may be hospitalized again or sent home the same day. If tolerated, these treatments can be repeated every 3 weeks for a set number of cycles. Tumor biopsy samples may be collected at various timepoints.
L79: #### Compensation
L80:   * This is a funded trial. All tests and treatments associated with the trial will be covered once a dog is enrolled.
L81:   * Complications associated with the trial will be covered. Clients are financially responsible for all treatments and diagnostics that are unrelated to the trial. Association between complications and trial treatment will be determined by the overseeing clinician and investigators.
L82:   * Initial evaluation appointments will be charged. For dogs accepted to the study, recheck exams during clinical trial appointments will be free of cost ($60 value per visit).
L83:   * CMP-002 (and PD-1 blockade, if included) treatment will be administered free of cost. Hospitalization immediately after CMP-002 administration and associated treatments will be free of cost. Blood sampling and tumor biopsies associated with the trial will be free of cost.
L84:   * One week after CMP-002, blood work will be needed. If performed at the MSU Veterinary Medical Center, the cost will be covered by the trial. If performed through your local veterinarian, you will be reimbursed up to $99 per test.
L85: Note: Test and treatments associated with the trial are covered for enrolled dogs. This does not include any surgical procedures.

protocol.name: Novel Treatment for Nasal Tumors
protocol.tagline: Help us treat nasal tumors in dogs using a new kind of therapy!
protocol.description:
Nasal tumors can cause severe nasal bleeding or discharge and difficulty breathing. These tumors often aggressively spread throughout the tissues of the nasal cavity and into the surrounding organs, including the eye and brain. Radiation therapy is the treatment of choice for nasal tumors in dogs; however, radiation therapy isn't often good for long-term control of the tumor. An another treatment option is transarterial embolization, or TAE, which involves the delivery of a mechanical “clot” to the main arteries supplying blood to the tissues of the nasal cavity with the goal of eliminating the blood supply of the tumor and decreasing tumor size.

The purposes of this study are to 1) describe TAE in dogs with naturally-occurring nasal cancer, 2) evaluate the effect that nasal TAE has on the tumor, and 3) evaluate the effect that nasal TAE has on the values measured by positron emission tomography (PET) scanning.

protocol.name: Assessing a new technique to shrink liver tumors in dogs
protocol.tagline: Help us learn more about this new technique that could shrink liver tumors in dogs!
protocol.description:
When liver tumors in dogs cannot be removed with surgery, treatment options are limited or non-existent. In humans, one of the standard treatments for those cases is transarterial chemoembolization (TACE), which eliminates the blood supply of the tumor and may decrease tumor size. The objectives of this study are to 1) describe the procedure of TACE  using a novel treatment agent in a group of dogs with naturally-occurring liver cancer, and 2) evaluate the effect that liver TACE has on clinical signs, size and viability of the tumor.

Demonstrating the feasibility and efficacy of liver TACE to improve clinical signs and decrease tumor size and volume can significantly advance our treatment of this difficult disease process, as current treatment options are limited and lack efficacy. Additionally, liver TACE is minimally invasive and provides many potential advantages over traditional surgical therapies.

protocol.requirements: Day 0: Patients will have an oncology exam, blood collection, and urine collection. Prior to this first appointment, owners will be asked to collect a fresh fecal sample from their pet at home to bring with them to this appointment. Radiation therapy under general anesthesia will also be started.Days 1 through 4: Each day, for a total of four days, cats will be placed under general anesthesia for approximately 20-30 minutes while radiation therapy is administered. Once they are awake and recovered from anesthesia, cats can be discharged to go home with their owners unless an overnight stay is indicated.2 weeks and 6 weeks post radiation therapy: Just like Day 0, cats will have an oncology exam, blood collection, and urine collection. Owners should bring a fresh sample of their cat’s feces to these appointments.
protocol.responsibilities: Pet owners are responsible for bringing their cat on time to each scheduled appointment. Owners will need to collect a fecal sample from their cat at home to bring to the Day 0 visit as well as the 2 and 6 weeks post therapy follow up visits. There will be a quality of life survey for owners to fill out electronically at each visit and every 2 months for up to 18 months (~ 1-2 min time commitment).
protocol.whoCan: We are looking to enroll:Cats with gastrointestinal small cell lymphoma confirmed with biopsy that are newly diagnosed but challenging to medicate or those that have relapsed (failed previous chemotherapy) will be eligible for enrollment. Within 14 days of enrollment, analysis of blood and urine will be needed to determine general health for treatment and anesthesia. Cats cannot have been given any chemotherapy or corticosteroids for at least 7 days before radiation therapy begins. Clients must live within a 6 hour drive from College Station Texas.
protocol.benefits: There are risks associated with general anesthesia and the radiation therapy treatment. These risks will be discussed with each owner before any cat is enrolled.
protocol.compensation:
Owners are responsible for the costs associated with the blood and urine panels performed about14 days before enrollment to determine enrollment eligibility. 

Once enrolled in the study, all study-related costs are covered. If a cat needs to be housed overnight, there may be costs associated with housing in our hospital.
protocol.timeCommitment:
There are a total of 7 visits associated with this study. Days 0 and 1-4 will be day long appointments where radiation therapy is given under general anesthesia. In some instances, patients may stay overnight.

2 weeks and 6 weeks later, each visit can last anywhere from 2-4 hours.

protocol.name: Single Radiation Treatment for Dogs with Transmissible Venereal Tumor
protocol.description:
Canine transmissible venereal tumor (TVT) is an infectious cancer that can be spread between dogs, often through grooming behaviors or sexual contact. This cancer can be found worldwide, but is most common in Central and South America, Africa, and Asia. In the United States, this cancer is most commonly seen in animals rescued from other parts of the world, or in free-roaming pets in very remote areas.


Treatment for this cancer involves once-weekly injections of chemotherapy, which are given until the cancer is resolved. For patients who cannot undergo this chemotherapy treatment, finding alternate therapies can be invaluable. We know that this cancer responds well to older forms of radiation therapy; however, we aim to determine if a single treatment with modernized radiation can provide similar treatment outcomes with fewer visits compared to chemotherapy.
protocol.requirements: Dogs enrolled in this study will receive a single dose of radiation therapy, followed by recheck visits 7 days and 28 days after treatment. At each of these visits, patients will have tumor measurements and small samples of their masses collected with a needle for analysis. Patients complete the study on day 28 or if their tumor progresses before the end of the study. At that time, patients with persistent tumors are eligible to receive $1000 towards the cost of standard chemotherapy treatment.
protocol.responsibilities: Owners must return to CSU for the described recheck visits following entry into the study. These include the day of radiation treatment, as well as visits 1 week and 4 weeks after radiation therapy. They are also responsible for the costs of the pre-enrollment examination and to confirm the diagnosis of transmissible venereal tumor.
protocol.whoCan: Confirmed diagnosis of TVT with at least one lesion > 1 cm in size and amenable to repeated measurement and samplingHealthy enough to undergo general anesthesiaNo prior surgery, radiation, or systemic chemotherapy for treatment of primary tumorNo advanced cancer spread7-day washout from immunosuppressive medications
protocol.benefits: Possible benefits include shrinkage or resolution of the tumor. Risks of anesthesia include a decrease in heart rate, decrease in blood pressure, vomiting, risk of aspiration pneumonia, and sudden death. Few to no side effects are expected with this radiation treatment. Possible short-term side effects could include irritation to the mucous membranes and skin. Rare, long-term side effects could include loss of fur, change in fur color, and mild thickening or scarring of the tissues in area of radiation treatment.
protocol.compensation: The study pays for recheck examination fees, pre-treatment complete blood count and biochemistry profile, abdominal x-ray or ultrasound prior to treatment if needed, and all costs related to radiation planning and treatment. If the tumor progresses during the course of the study or is still present at study end, a $1000 credit will be applied to the patient's account to be put towards the costs of additional treatment.
protocol.timeCommitment: There are 3 visits associated with this clinical trial: one for radiation treatment and then recheck visits 7 and 28 days after radiation. Pets will likely be at the hospital for most of the day at the first visit. The other two visits should take 1-2 hours each.

protocol.name: Advancing Non-Invasive Care for Dogs with Lymphoma
protocol.tagline: Exploring a non-invasive, non-chemotherapy option to target lymphoma tumors.
protocol.description:
Canine lymphoma is a common cancer in dogs that often affects lymph nodes. While chemotherapy remains an established treatment, researchers are exploring additional approaches.


This study is evaluating the safety and feasibility of High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound (HIFU), a non-invasive technology that uses focused sound waves to destroy targeted tumor tissue for canine lymphoma. Beyond killing a portion of the tumor cells in the lymph node, this treatment may help stimulate the immune system to recognize cancer cells.
protocol.requirements: Participation involves approximately 3–4 hospital visits over a 30-day period. Dogs enrolled in the study will receive veterinary examinations, laboratory testing, and medical imaging.On the treatment day, HIFU will be used to treat a targeted lymph node. Sedation and/or general anesthesia will be required for the procedure.Beginning 8 days after the HIFU procedure, the dog will receive doxorubicin chemotherapy. The study covers the cost of five doxorubicin chemotherapy treatments, an established treatment option for canine lymphoma.
protocol.whoCan: We are looking for dogs that have: Confirmed diagnosis of nodal B or T cell lymphoma Targeted lymph node is prescapular (in front of the shoulder blade) or popliteal (behind the knee)
protocol.benefits: Participation may help researchers learn more about the potential use of focused ultrasound for canine lymphoma and could contribute to improved treatment options for pets in the future.Possible side effects from the HIFU treatment are generally expected to be mild to moderate and may include tiredness, soreness near the treated area, and swelling. Some dogs may also experience skin irritation, mild burns, or small sores or scabs over the treated area.
protocol.compensation: All study-related costs are covered by the study sponsor, including medical imaging, bloodwork, HIFU treatment, and five doxorubicin chemotherapy treatments.
protocol.timeCommitment: A month period with 3-4 hospital visits.
